newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals--Japan aluminium demand seen strong.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals--Japan aluminium demand seen strong.

text.p: Japanese demand for aluminium has remained strong so far this year, despite weak statistics from aluminium-using sectors that, as feared, followed the country's sales tax increase in April, traders said on Wednesday.
"So far demand has not dropped as expected. We're all puzzled," said one trader. "Although the official statistics have shown a decline, we haven't seen clear evidence of that."

Traders were waiting nervously for signs of a slow-down in Japanese demand after the metal's premiums in term contracts for the July-September quarter settled at $86-90 per tonne, five dollars above levels seen in the prior quarter.
Data released on Monday showed May domestic vehicle sales in Japan fell 9.4 percent from the same month a year earlier, the second consecutive month of year-on-year declines.
Japanese April housing starts released last Friday sank 9.3 percent, the fourth consecutive year-on-year fall.

In contrast to this, Japan's aluminium spot premiums remained high, above $90 per tonne, suggesting that aluminium demand was still strong. Traders said some deals were done above $100 for delivery this month.

In the nickel market, a strike at Inco Ltd has sparked worries among some Japanese users, especially battery firms, as the Canadian giant is the sole provider of nickel powder suitable for making nickel-cadmium batteries.

"You can use only Inco nickel powder for production of nickel-cadmium batteries," said a trader at one of Japan's major trading houses. "If the shipments stop, there'll be a serious problem, though I would think Inco would put top priority on nickel powder deliveries."

Traders estimated Japan purchased about 8,000 tonnes of nickel powder from Inco last year but only 3,000 tonnes of refined nickel, as Inco's high-grade metal was not used for stainless-steel production.
On Tuesday, about 4,670 union workers at Inco, the world's second-largest nickel maker, went on strike after voting down a tentative contract agreement reached on Friday.
Company and union officials said they did not know when talks would resume.
The news boosted nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Tuesday, particularly as it came on the heels of a price decline triggered by the tentative contract.

The physical copper and zinc markets remained quiet following heavy imports under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) scheme in April. Spot premiums for the two metals were flat at $60-70 per tonne and $40-85 per tonne, respectively.
Japanese traders also expressed doubts about rumours that China might sell copper from its strategic stockpile into the market. The rumours were denied by China's Central Reserve Bureau.
"I don't think it's going to happen," said one trader at a major Japanese trading house.

He said it was obvious that China needed the metal in the future, and Beijing was also unlikely to lend its copper reserves to the market, as it did in 1995, because such deals would no longer bring large profits.
Zinc traders saw abundant offers from China seeking to capitalise on the metal's current high international prices, but they added there were few deals being made.
